lines.text: Hourly pay rose 3.1%. Prices rose 3.4%.
lines.say: Hourly pay rose three point one percent. Prices rose three point four.

lines.text: In the year to August 2026, that left real hourly pay down 0.3%.
lines.say: In the year to August twenty twenty-six, that left real hourly pay down three tenths of a percent.

lines.text: A raise smaller than inflation is a pay cut that never shows up on your pay stub.
lines.say: A raise that's smaller than inflation is a pay cut that never shows up on your pay stub.

lines.text: Prices won that round, by three tenths of a point.
lines.say: Prices won that round, by three tenths of a point.

lines.text: Over decades it adds up. What cost $1 in 1970 cost about $8.30 in 2025.
lines.say: Over decades, it adds up. By the government's index, what cost one dollar in nineteen seventy cost about eight dollars and thirty cents in twenty twenty-five.

lines.text: Flip it: a 2025 dollar buys what about 12 cents bought in 1970.
lines.say: Flip it around, and a twenty twenty-five dollar buys what about twelve cents bought in nineteen seventy.

lines.text: So where does inflation come from, and what do people actually do about it?
lines.say: So where does inflation come from, and what do people actually do about it?

lines.text: Real data from the BLS, the Fed and the Treasury, one example with exact math. Education, not advice.

lines.text: Chapter 1: What inflation actually is
lines.say: Chapter one: what inflation actually is.

lines.text: Inflation is a broad, lasting rise in prices. Flip side: each dollar buys less.
lines.say: Inflation is a broad, lasting rise in prices. The flip side is that each dollar buys a little less.

lines.text: One pricey item isn't inflation. If eggs jump but TVs fall, the average may barely move.
lines.say: One pricey item isn't inflation. If eggs jump but TVs get cheaper, the average may barely move.

lines.text: The main US gauge is the Consumer Price Index, or CPI, from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
lines.say: The main US gauge is the Consumer Price Index, or C P I, from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

lines.text: Every month, the BLS prices a basket of what city households buy: housing, food, gas, medical care and more.
lines.say: Every month, the BLS prices a basket of what city households buy: housing, food, gas, medical care and more.

lines.text: Housing is the biggest slice, so rent and home costs move the number a lot.
lines.say: Housing is the biggest slice, so rent and home costs move the number a lot.

lines.text: In the August 2026 CPI, prices were up 3.4% from a year earlier.
lines.say: In the August twenty twenty-six report, prices were up three point four percent from a year earlier.

lines.text: New CPI data comes out every month, so by the time you watch, there's a newer number.
lines.say: New CPI data comes out every month, so by the time you watch this, there's a newer number.

lines.text: Strip out food and energy, which jump around, and you get core inflation: 2.4% over the same 12 months.
lines.say: Strip out food and energy, which jump around, and you get core inflation: two point four percent over the same twelve months.

lines.text: Most of that gap is gasoline, up 27.4% in a year.
lines.say: Most of that gap is gasoline, which was up twenty-seven point four percent in a year.

lines.text: The Federal Reserve aims for 2% inflation over the long run, an official goal since January 2012.
lines.say: The Federal Reserve aims for two percent inflation over the long run. That's been its official goal since January twenty twelve.

lines.text: Why not zero? Falling prices can make people delay buying and make debts heavier.
lines.say: Why not zero? Falling prices can make people put off buying, and they make debts heavier.

lines.text: Two words to know: nominal is the number on the label. Real is that number after inflation.
lines.say: Two words to know. Nominal is the number on the label. Real is that number after inflation.

lines.text: Rough rule: real equals nominal minus inflation. That's how a 3.1% raise became -0.3%.
lines.say: The rough rule is real equals nominal minus inflation. That's how a three point one percent raise turned into minus three tenths.

lines.text: Chapter 2: Where inflation comes from
lines.say: Chapter two: where inflation comes from.

lines.text: Cause one is demand: everyone trying to buy more than the economy can make right now.
lines.say: Cause one is demand: everyone trying to buy more than the economy can make right now.

lines.text: Economists sum it up as too much money chasing too few goods.
lines.say: Economists sum it up as too much money chasing too few goods.

lines.text: In 2020, as relief programs and the Fed pumped cash into the economy, the M2 money supply grew about 25%.
lines.say: In twenty twenty, as relief programs and the Fed pumped cash into the economy, the M2 money supply grew about twenty-five percent.

lines.text: When the economy reopened, all that spending hit factories and shipping lines that couldn't keep up.
lines.say: When the economy reopened, that spending hit factories and shipping lines that couldn't keep up.

lines.text: Cause two is costs: when it costs more to make or ship things, sellers pass part of it on.
lines.say: Cause two is costs. When it costs more to make or ship things, sellers pass part of that on to you.

lines.text: Energy is the classic example. In the 12 months ending June 2022, energy prices jumped 41.6%.
lines.say: Energy is the classic example. In the twelve months ending June twenty twenty-two, energy prices jumped forty-one point six percent.

lines.text: And oil is priced globally, so a spike hits almost every country at once.
lines.say: And oil is priced globally, so a spike hits almost every country at the same time.

lines.text: It happened again in 2026, with oil back above $100 a barrel.
lines.say: It happened again in twenty twenty-six, with oil back above a hundred dollars a barrel.

lines.text: Cause three is money itself. If money grows much faster than the stuff to buy, each dollar is worth less.
lines.say: Cause three is money itself. If money grows much faster than the stuff there is to buy, each dollar is worth less.

lines.text: Milton Friedman: "Inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon."
lines.say: The economist Milton Friedman put it this way: inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon.

scene.text: Inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon.

lines.text: That's one school of thought. Other economists put more weight on demand and supply shocks.
lines.say: That's one school of thought. Other economists put more weight on demand and on supply shocks.

lines.text: Cause four is sneaky: expectations. If everyone expects prices to rise, they act in ways that make it happen.
lines.say: Cause four is sneaky: expectations. If everyone expects prices to rise, they act in ways that make it happen.

lines.text: Example: workers expect 5% inflation and ask for 5% raises. Businesses pay it, then raise prices 5%.
lines.say: Say workers expect five percent inflation, so they ask for five percent raises. Businesses pay it, then raise prices five percent.

lines.text: That's why the Fed works to keep expectations anchored near 2%. Once they slip, they're hard to pull back.
lines.say: That's why the Fed works to keep expectations anchored near two percent. Once they slip, they're hard to pull back.

lines.text: The Fed's main tool is interest rates. Higher rates make borrowing pricier, which cools spending and, with a lag, prices.
lines.say: The Fed's main tool is interest rates. Higher rates make borrowing pricier, which cools spending and, with a lag, prices.

lines.text: In September 2026, the Fed raised its target range by a quarter point to 3.75% to 4%, its first hike since 2023.
lines.say: In September twenty twenty-six, the Fed raised its target range a quarter point, to three point seven five to four percent, its first hike since twenty twenty-three.

lines.text: The Fed meets about every six weeks, so the current rate may differ.
lines.say: The Fed meets about every six weeks, so the current rate may already be different.

lines.text: Chapter 3: Fifty years of inflation
lines.say: Chapter three: fifty years of inflation.

lines.text: Here's US inflation from 1970 to 1985, as yearly averages from the BLS.
lines.say: Here's US inflation from nineteen seventy to nineteen eighty-five, as yearly averages from the BLS.

lines.text: It peaked at 13.5% in 1980, averaged over the whole year.
lines.say: It peaked at thirteen and a half percent in nineteen eighty, averaged over the whole year.

lines.text: Oil shocks in 1973 and 1979 poured fuel on it. In 1979, Paul Volcker took over the Fed.
lines.say: Oil shocks in nineteen seventy-three and nineteen seventy-nine poured fuel on it. Then in nineteen seventy-nine, Paul Volcker took over the Fed.

lines.text: His Fed let short-term rates climb to a record 20% in late 1980.
lines.say: His Fed let short-term rates climb to a record twenty percent in late nineteen eighty.

lines.text: It worked, but it hurt. Unemployment hit 10.8% in November 1982.
lines.say: It worked, but it hurt. Unemployment hit ten point eight percent in November nineteen eighty-two.

lines.text: By 1983, yearly inflation was down to 3.2%.
lines.say: By nineteen eighty-three, yearly inflation was down to three point two percent.

lines.text: The lesson central bankers took: inflation is easy to start and painful to stop.
lines.say: The lesson central bankers took: inflation is easy to start and painful to stop.

lines.text: Then came calm. From 2015 to 2020, yearly inflation stayed between 0.1% and 2.4%.
lines.say: Then came calm. From twenty fifteen to twenty twenty, yearly inflation stayed between zero point one and two point four percent.

lines.text: Then it jumped: 4.7% in 2021 and 8% for 2022 as a whole.
lines.say: Then it jumped: four point seven percent in twenty twenty-one, and eight percent for twenty twenty-two as a whole.

lines.text: The peak: 9.1% for the 12 months ending June 2022, the biggest jump since 1981.
lines.say: The peak was nine point one percent for the twelve months ending June twenty twenty-two, the biggest jump since nineteen eighty-one.

lines.text: The Fed raised the top of its range from 0.25% in early 2022 to 5.5% by July 2023.
lines.say: The Fed raised the top of its target range from a quarter percent in early twenty twenty-two to five and a half percent by July twenty twenty-three.

lines.text: Inflation cooled to 2.9% in 2024 and 2.6% in 2025, still above the 2% goal.
lines.say: Inflation cooled to two point nine percent in twenty twenty-four and two point six in twenty twenty-five, still above the two percent goal.

lines.text: Then energy spiked again, and the 12-month rate hit 3.4% by August 2026.
lines.say: Then energy spiked again, and by August twenty twenty-six the twelve-month rate was back to three point four percent.

lines.text: Inflation even sets some raises. Social Security's COLA was 8.7% for 2023 and 2.8% for 2026.
lines.say: Inflation even sets some raises. Social Security's cost-of-living increase was eight point seven percent for twenty twenty-three, and two point eight percent for twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: Chapter 4: What it does to your money
lines.say: Chapter four: what it does to your money.

scene.title: What it does to your money

lines.text: Quick tool: the rule of 72. Divide 72 by the inflation rate to get roughly how many years until prices double.
lines.say: Here's a quick tool: the rule of seventy-two. Divide seventy-two by the inflation rate, and you get roughly how many years until prices double.

lines.text: At 2%, that's 36 years. At 3%, it's 24 years.
lines.say: At two percent, that's thirty-six years. At three percent, it's twenty-four years.

lines.text: At 9.1%, it's under 8 years: 72 divided by 9.1 is about 7.9.
lines.say: And at nine point one percent, it's under eight years, because seventy-two divided by nine point one is about seven point nine.

lines.text: Say you have $10,000 in savings paying 0.38%, the FDIC's national average as of August 2026.
lines.say: Say you have ten thousand dollars in a savings account paying zero point three eight percent. That's the FDIC's national average as of August twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: After a year, you'd have $10,038. Looks like a gain.
lines.say: After a year, you'd have ten thousand thirty-eight dollars. Looks like a gain.

lines.text: But prices rose 3.4% over 12 months. Divide by 1.034 and you get $9,707.93.
lines.say: But prices rose three point four percent over those twelve months. Divide by one point zero three four, and you get nine thousand seven hundred seven dollars and ninety-three cents.

lines.text: So your $10,038 buys what about $9,708 bought a year earlier.
lines.say: So your ten thousand thirty-eight dollars buys what about nine thousand seven hundred eight dollars bought a year earlier.

lines.text: At a hypothetical 4% instead: $10,400, about $10,058 in buying power. A $292 loss versus a $58 gain.
lines.say: At a hypothetical four percent instead, you'd have ten thousand four hundred, about ten thousand fifty-eight in buying power. A loss of about two hundred ninety-two dollars, versus a gain of about fifty-eight.

lines.text: Same money, same year. The difference is whether the rate beats inflation.
lines.say: Same money, same year. The only difference is whether the rate beats inflation.

lines.text: Shortcut: 0.38% minus 3.4% is a real return of about -3%.
lines.say: The shortcut: zero point three eight percent minus three point four is a real return of about minus three percent.

lines.text: And inflation doesn't hit everyone the same way.
lines.say: And inflation doesn't hit everyone the same way.

lines.text: Take a hypothetical fixed mortgage payment of $1,500. Ten years later, it's still $1,500.
lines.say: Take a hypothetical fixed mortgage payment of fifteen hundred dollars a month. Ten years later, it's still fifteen hundred.

lines.text: If prices rise 3.4% a year for those 10 years, that $1,500 feels like about $1,074 in today's dollars.
lines.say: If prices rose three point four percent a year for those ten years, that fifteen hundred would feel like about one thousand seventy-four in today's dollars.

lines.text: The flip side: variable-rate debt, like most credit cards, can get pricier when the Fed raises rates.
lines.say: The flip side is variable-rate debt, like most credit cards, which can get pricier when the Fed raises rates.

lines.text: For workers, average hourly pay rose 3.1% in the year to August 2026, the slowest since May 2021, per Trading Economics.
lines.say: For workers, average hourly pay rose three point one percent in the year to August twenty twenty-six, the slowest since May twenty twenty-one, per Trading Economics.

lines.text: Chapter 5: Tools people use against it
lines.say: Chapter five: tools people use against it.

lines.text: These are tools people use, not recommendations. Every one has trade-offs.
lines.say: These are tools people use, not recommendations. Every one of them has trade-offs.

lines.text: Tool one: the rate on your cash. Bank rates vary a lot; many people compare theirs to inflation, like 0.38% vs. 3.4% in August.
lines.say: Tool one is the simplest: the rate on your cash. Bank rates vary a lot, and many people compare theirs to inflation, like that zero point three eight versus three point four.

lines.text: Tool two: Series I savings bonds, sold by the US Treasury at TreasuryDirect.
lines.say: Tool two is Series I savings bonds, sold by the US Treasury at TreasuryDirect.

lines.text: An I bond's rate has two parts: a fixed rate that never changes, and an inflation rate that resets every six months.
lines.say: An I bond's rate has two parts: a fixed rate that never changes, and an inflation rate that resets every six months.

lines.text: For I bonds bought May through October 2026, the combined rate was 4.26%.
lines.say: For I bonds bought from May through October twenty twenty-six, the combined rate was four point two six percent.

lines.text: That's a 0.90% fixed rate plus 3.34% annualized inflation, plus a tiny bit from combining them.
lines.say: That's a zero point nine percent fixed rate, plus three point three four percent annualized inflation, plus a tiny bit from combining the two.

lines.text: Treasury sets new rates every May 1 and November 1, so bonds bought from November 2026 to April 2027 get a different rate.
lines.say: Treasury sets new rates every May first and November first, so bonds bought from November twenty twenty-six through April twenty twenty-seven get a different rate.

lines.text: The rules: up to $10,000 a year per person, no cashing out in year one, and cashing out before 5 years costs 3 months of interest.
lines.say: The rules: up to ten thousand dollars a year per person, no cashing out in the first year, and cashing out before five years costs three months of interest.

lines.text: Tool three: TIPS, Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities, in 5, 10 and 30-year terms.
lines.say: Tool three is TIPS, Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities, in five, ten and thirty-year terms.

lines.text: With TIPS, the principal rises with the CPI, and a fixed interest rate is paid on that bigger principal every six months.
lines.say: With TIPS, the principal itself rises with the CPI, and a fixed interest rate gets paid on that bigger principal every six months.

lines.text: Hypothetical: $10,000 of TIPS, and prices rise 3% in a year. The principal becomes $10,300.
lines.say: Hypothetically, say you hold ten thousand dollars of TIPS, and prices rise three percent in a year. The principal becomes ten thousand three hundred.

lines.text: At a hypothetical 2% rate, a year of interest is $206 instead of $200.
lines.say: At a hypothetical two percent rate, a year of interest is two hundred six dollars instead of two hundred.

lines.text: Hold to maturity and you get the greater of the adjusted or original principal. Sell early and the price can be lower.
lines.say: Hold to maturity, and you get the greater of the adjusted or the original principal. Sell early, and the market price can be lower.

lines.text: Key difference: I bonds have a yearly cap and can't be resold. TIPS trade in the market, so prices move.
lines.say: The key difference: I bonds have that yearly cap and can't be resold, while TIPS trade in the market, so their prices move.

lines.text: Tool four is on the debt side: a fixed-rate loan locks the payment while prices rise, like that mortgage example.
lines.say: Tool four is on the debt side. A fixed-rate loan locks the payment while prices rise, like that mortgage example.

lines.text: Some income adjusts on its own. Social Security's COLA compares July-September CPI-W with a year earlier.
lines.say: Some income adjusts on its own. Social Security's cost-of-living raise compares the July through September C P I W with a year earlier.

lines.text: Each year's COLA is announced in the fall and first shows up in January checks.
lines.say: Each year's raise is announced in the fall, and it first shows up in January checks.

lines.text: Others hold long-term assets like stocks or real estate, which can rise with prices over long stretches but can also fall hard.
lines.say: Others hold long-term assets like stocks or real estate, which can rise with prices over long stretches but can also fall hard.

lines.text: Chapter 6: The recap
lines.say: Chapter six: the recap.

lines.text: Inflation means each dollar buys less. The CPI tracks it monthly, and the Fed aims for 2%.
lines.say: Inflation means each dollar buys less. The CPI tracks it every month, and the Fed aims for two percent.

lines.text: It comes from too much demand, higher costs, faster money growth and expectations.
lines.say: It comes from too much demand, higher costs, faster money growth and expectations.

lines.text: What matters is the real number: your raise or your interest rate, minus inflation.
lines.say: What matters is the real number: your raise or your interest rate, minus inflation.

lines.text: Savings rates, I bonds, TIPS and fixed-rate debt each handle it differently, with trade-offs.
lines.say: And savings rates, I bonds, TIPS and fixed-rate debt each handle it differently, with their own trade-offs.

lines.text: Remember where we started: pay up 3.1%, prices up 3.4%.
lines.say: Remember where we started: pay up three point one percent, prices up three point four.

lines.text: A raise isn't really a raise until it beats inflation.
lines.say: A raise isn't really a raise until it beats inflation.

post.yt_desc:
In the year to August 2026, average hourly pay rose 3.1% while consumer prices rose 3.4%, so real hourly pay fell 0.3%. This video explains inflation from zero: how the BLS measures it with the CPI, why the Fed aims for 2%, the four big causes (demand, costs, money and expectations), and 50 years of history from the 1970s and Paul Volcker to the 9.1% peak in June 2022 and the Fed's September 2026 hike. It works through a hypothetical $10,000 savings example with exact math, the rule of 72, and how I bonds, TIPS, fixed-rate debt and Social Security's COLA handle inflation.

Sources: BLS Consumer Price Index and Real Earnings releases for August 2026 (Sep 11, 2026) and June 2022 (Jul 13, 2022); BLS CPI-U annual averages; Federal Reserve, Statement on Longer-Run Goals (Jan 2012); Federal Reserve History, Volcker's anti-inflation measures; Reuters and Trading Economics (Sep 2026); Atlanta Fed (May 2021) on M2; TreasuryDirect I bond rate release (May 1, 2026) and TIPS page; SSA COLA announcement (Oct 2025); FDIC national rates (Aug 2026); Milton Friedman (1963).

News and education, not financial advice.
